title: Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders
one_liner: Turn the vet's preg-check clipboard into a borrower-consented, third-party-verified herd inventory that banks can lend against.
customer: Community banks, Farm Credit associations and ag lenders with cattle loan books (they require it or pay per report, usually passed through to the borrower). Secondary payer is the cow-calf or heifer-development operator who wants bigger operating lines or bred-heifer financing on better terms.
problem: Cattle collateral has no VIN. Lenders verify with drive-by counts and borrower-supplied spreadsheets, and prosecutors in 2026 alleged a roughly $9.4M fraud that included a loan of $2.8M against 850 head. Farm loan delinquencies are rising while bred cows trade around $3,000+ per head, so a 500-cow borrower is $1.5M+ of collateral that nobody independent has counted.
solution: A 'Verified Herd Report' generated at the working day the vet is already doing. The vet or tech logs every head with an EID or visual tag scan (a $500 handheld reader plus a phone app), age class, pregnancy status and stage, and location. The vet e-signs and the borrower approves sharing with one tap. The lender gets a portal with timestamped, geotagged counts and year-over-year flags (head count down, pregnancy rate down, tags not matching last year). A second light pass happens at weaning. The vet earns a per-head fee for data they already write down and throw in the truck door pocket.
why_now: Federal EID ear tags became mandatory for many interstate cattle movements in Nov 2024, so per-head digital ID is now normal and cheap. Herd rebuilding at record cattle prices is being financed with debt, lenders entered 2026 carrying operating losses from 2023-2025 (rising delinquencies and restructures), and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case is making ag loan committees ask for verification. Fall preg-check season is running right now (Sept-Nov).
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split roughly 50/50 with the vet practice, charged to the borrower or the lender as a loan condition. Add a portfolio dashboard for lenders at $500-2,000 per month once an institution has 100+ verified borrowers. Later, sell the verified inventory and pregnancy data to lenders as an underwriting input (advance rates on verified bred heifers).
non_obvious_insight: The vet is the only independent professional who physically handles every animal in the herd once or twice a year. They count, tag-check and pregnancy-check every cow, and that data dies on a clipboard. Vets refuse to police clients, but they will happily attest to what they handled when the borrower initiates the request, so the conflict-of-interest problem disappears. Honest borrowers are the real buyers: verified bred females can justify higher advance rates, and that cheap capital funds the fee many times over.
first_30_days: Preg-check season is live, so sign up 3 rural practices that each do several thousand head of fall preg-checks. Pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders (target the one who has been burned by a herd count before; work through state bankers' association ag committees). Run a pilot on about 10 willing borrowers with a form-based app and a PDF report, charging $2/head. Gather a before and after on what the lender learned that the drive-by inspection missed, then use that to sell the annual program.

tournament.cluster: Lenders and investors unable to verify collateral exists
judge_notes: operator: rank 3/25 - Live fraud case, preg-check season now, vets already handle every animal; per-head fee and a tight pilot.
vc: rank 2/25 - Sharp wedge: vets already handle every head; lenders burned by fraud; fall preg-check season now; per-head revenue with real data moat.
contrarian: rank 1/24 - Vet is the only independent party touching every cow. Live fraud case, EID tags, and preg-check season make it testable now.

competitors.name: CattleMax
competitors.what_they_do: Cloud cattle record-keeping software with inventory, pregnancy and breeding records, RFID-reader integration and income/expense tracking. Its homepage and pricing page (fetched) mention no lender/bank reports and no vet data sharing.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Calls itself 'North America's Most Widely Used Cattle Software'. Pricing is $30/mo (Commercial) and $41/mo (Registered) for up to 250 head, and custom above 2,000 head. Funding not found.

competitors.name: AgriWebb
competitors.what_they_do: Livestock management software (movements, performance, cost of production, map) with hardware integrations. The homepage does not mention lender sharing or third-party verified counts.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Over 17,000 producers and more than 25% of Australia's grazing animals, per its site. Funding not found.

competitors.name: IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport)
competitors.what_they_do: USDA-approved third-party verification of cattle age/source, breed, feed and sustainability claims, plus EID tags. 'Beef Passport' ties each EID to its verification records. Nothing on lender or herd-inventory verification appeared. This is the closest 'independent verifier with an EID data platform' and could add lender reports as a feature.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Part of Where Food Comes From, a publicly traded verification company. Funding details not fetched.

competitors.name: Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence)
competitors.what_they_do: Owns EID tag/reader hardware and cattle data platforms. The pages returned HTTP 403, so I could not confirm any lender or collateral offering. Big-vendor entry into 'verified inventory' is a plausible incumbent risk.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Subsidiary of Merck & Co.; vet-channel distribution is already in place. Page not read.

competitors.name: Ceres Tag
competitors.what_they_do: Solar-powered satellite GPS ear tags for real-time location and behavior. It pitches traceability and supply-chain credibility, but the homepage mentions no lender or collateral use case. Continuous tracking is a different route to 'verified head count'.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Says it operates in more than 30 countries. Funding not shown.

competitors.name: Halter
competitors.what_they_do: GPS collars, virtual fencing and herd monitoring for dairy and beef. The homepage mentions no lending or collateral features.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Operates in the US, Canada, Australia, NZ, Argentina and Uruguay. Funding not shown on the page.

competitors.name: HerdDogg
competitors.what_they_do: Bluetooth smart ear tags for health and heat detection at about 8 cents/day per animal. No lender or inventory-verification angle appeared.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Scale and funding not stated on the page.

competitors.name: Gallagher Animal Management
competitors.what_they_do: EID readers, scale heads and the Animal Performance software. The page mentions no lender reports or third-party verification.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established global hardware vendor; pricing not on the page.

competition.white_space:
Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.

The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature.
competition.evidence_of_demand: None verified this session, because I could not run searches. Two specific claims in the idea are unconfirmed: the '2026 roughly $9.4M fraud, including a $2.8M loan against 850 head', and the Nov 2024 federal EID rule. The EID claim is consistent with my prior knowledge but my APHIS fetch returned 404 (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/traceability/cattle). The Eastern Livestock Wikipedia fetch also returned 404. The OCC Agricultural Lending handbook PDF (https://www.occ.gov/publications-and-resources/publications/comptrollers-handbook/files/agricultural-lending/pub-ch-agricultural-lending.pdf) fetched but did not extract as readable text. Farm Credit's homepage (https://www.farmcredit.com/) shows no verification tooling. It is background knowledge, not something I confirmed here, that lenders already do collateral inspections and that historic cattle-collateral frauds such as Eastern Livestock (2010) exist. That points to real spend on manual workarounds, but the founder should confirm it with lender interviews. No RFPs, forum complaints or paid-service pricing were found.
competition.kill_reason: n/a. Nothing found shows a dominant or crowded direct competitor. The evidence is thin because no web searches were possible, so this is a provisional not-killed verdict pending a proper competitor search.
competition.sharper_angle: Skip the vet-as-attestor framing and sell to the lender as a covenant-compliance tool. Give the loan officer an 'inventory attestation' workflow they attach to the loan agreement, with three parts. (1) Accept attestations from any credible chute-side handler (vet, brand inspector, sale-barn or feedyard records, EID reader logs), not only vets, so a vet's reluctance does not block the product. (2) Reconcile each attestation against independent sources: the lender's prior-year counts, sale-barn and movement records, and EID or CVI data. The output is a reconciled 'expected vs. attested head' variance flag, which is what catches fraud. (3) Track the lien and ownership side (UCC and brand records) next to the count. Start with a single community-bank or Farm Credit association pilot that makes it a condition on new bred-heifer and operating-line loans. Have the bank pay, priced per loan or per portfolio, to avoid the 'honest borrower must opt in' adverse-selection trap. Before building, run 10-15 lender and vet interviews and a proper search for existing third-party inspection vendors. Also test whether IMI Global/WFCF (Beef Passport) or a big EID vendor would white-label this.
